## Description

This vignette shows how to add sampling bias to a prediction using functions in the `nicheR` package. Real data are rarely collected evenly. Sites near roads, cities, or well-studied areas are visited more often, so the data show where people looked as well as where conditions are suitable. In `nicheR`, this uneven effort is represented with a bias surface that is combined with the prediction of a niche.

The main functions used in this vignette are:

- `prepare_bias()`: standardizes one or more layers that represent sampling effort and combines them into one bias surface.
- `apply_bias()`: turns a prediction into a sampling weight and multiplies it by the bias surface.

Sampling effort changes from place to place, so these functions work only with raster layers (spatial mode). For the ideas behind this step, see [Sampling bias](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/concepts.html#sampling-bias) in the Concepts vignette.

<br>

## Getting ready

If `nicheR` has not been installed yet, please do so. See the [Main guide](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/index.html) for installation instructions.

Use the following lines of code to load `nicheR` and other packages needed for this vignette, and to set a working directory (if necessary).

<u>Note</u>: We will display functions from other packages as `package::function()`.

```{r get_ready, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Load packages
library(nicheR)
library(terra)

# Current directory
getwd()

# Define new directory
#setwd("YOUR/DIRECTORY")  # modify if setting a new directory

# Saving original plotting parameters
original_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
```

<br>

## Loading example data

The lines of code below load the data used in this vignette. The data are included in the `nicheR` package and consist of a prediction of the reference niche for part of the Americas, and two raster layers that we will use to represent sampling effort. The reference niche is defined by two environmental variables (bio1: Mean Annual Temperature and bio12: Annual Precipitation). It was built with `cl = 0.99` instead of the default 0.95, so its boundary reaches the ranges it was built from (see [The niche as an ellipsoid](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/concepts.html#the-niche-as-an-ellipsoid)). For details on how the prediction was obtained, see the vignette [2. Make a prediction](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/predict.html).

```{r data}
# Prediction of the reference niche
pred_rast <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "predictions_rast.tif",
                                     package = "nicheR"))

# Layers that represent sampling effort
bias_layers <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "ma_biases.tif",
                                       package = "nicheR"))
```

<br>

Let's take a look at both objects to get familiar with them.

```{r data_check}
# Layers in the prediction
names(pred_rast)

# Check the bias layers
bias_layers
```

<br>

The prediction has the two environmental variables and the four outputs of `predict()`. The bias layers are the number of species recorded (`sp_richness`) and the brightness of lights at night (`nighttime`). Let's plot them.

```{r data_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting area parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = 0.7)
marsr <- c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 4)

# Plots
terra::plot(bias_layers[["sp_richness"]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Species Richness")

terra::plot(bias_layers[["nighttime"]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Nighttime Lights")
```

<br>

## Preparing the bias surface

The two layers come in different units and scales. The `prepare_bias()` function puts them on a common scale and combines them. For each layer, the function:

1. Aligns the layer to a common grid.
2. Standardizes its values to go from 0 to 1.
3. Applies the direction of its effect. With `"direct"`, higher values mean more sampling effort. With `"inverse"`, higher values mean less effort, so the values are flipped as 1 minus the standardized value.

The layers are then multiplied to obtain one composite surface.

In our example, we will assume that sites with more recorded species have been visited more often, so richness has a direct effect. We will also assume that collectors stay away from the brightest sites, so nighttime lights have an inverse effect.

```{r prepare}
# Preparing the bias surface
bias_prep <- prepare_bias(bias_surface = bias_layers,
                          effect_direction = c("direct", "inverse"))

# Elements in the result
names(bias_prep)

# How the layers were combined
bias_prep$combination_formula
```

<br>

The result is a list. The element `composite_surface` is the bias surface, a `SpatRaster` with values from 0 to 1, and `combination_formula` keeps a record of how it was calculated. Let's plot the bias surface.

```{r prepare_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting the bias surface
par(cex = 0.7)

terra::plot(bias_prep$composite_surface,
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Composite Bias Surface")
```

<br>

Sites with high values are the ones most likely to be sampled. In our example, those are sites with many recorded species and little light at night, most of them in the south of the region. A value of 0 means that a site is never sampled.

<br>

### Effect of the direction

To see what the direction does to each layer, we can ask `prepare_bias()` to also return the layers after they were standardized. This is done with the argument `include_processed_layers`.

```{r direction}
# Preparing the bias surface and keeping the standardized layers
bias_steps <- prepare_bias(bias_surface = bias_layers,
                           effect_direction = c("direct", "inverse"),
                           include_processed_layers = TRUE,
                           verbose = FALSE)

# Names of the standardized layers
names(bias_steps$processed_layers)
```

<br>

Let's plot the two standardized layers.

```{r direction_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting area parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = 0.7)

# Plots
terra::plot(bias_steps$processed_layers[[1]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Richness (direct)")

terra::plot(bias_steps$processed_layers[[2]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Nighttime Lights (inverse)")
```

<br>

Richness keeps its pattern, now on a scale from 0 to 1. Nighttime lights are flipped. Most of the region is dark at night, so it stays close to 1, and only the brightest sites drop toward 0. The composite surface shown before is the product of these two layers.

Play with the values of `effect_direction` to see how the composite surface changes. Keep in mind that one direction is needed for each layer, in the same order as the layers. If only one direction is given, it is used for all the layers.

<br>

### Effect of the floor argument

In the composite surface, a few sites have values of 0 or close to it, and those sites will almost never be sampled. The argument `floor` sets a minimum value for the bias surface, so every site keeps at least a small chance of being sampled.

```{r floor}
# Preparing the bias surface with a minimum value
bias_floor <- prepare_bias(bias_surface = bias_layers,
                           effect_direction = c("direct", "inverse"),
                           floor = 0.05,
                           verbose = FALSE)

# Range of values without a floor
terra::global(bias_prep$composite_surface, fun = c("min", "max"),
              na.rm = TRUE)

# Range of values with a floor
terra::global(bias_floor$composite_surface, fun = c("min", "max"),
              na.rm = TRUE)
```

<br>

As you can see, the lowest value is now the one we set with `floor`. All the values that were above it stay the same.

The `prepare_bias()` function has other arguments that control the grid used to align the layers (`template_layer`) and how cells with missing values are treated (`mask_na`). See `?prepare_bias` for details.

<br>

## Applying bias to a prediction

The `apply_bias()` function combines the bias surface with a prediction in two steps. First, the prediction is turned into a sampling weight, the same way it is done in `sample_data()`. Second, that weight is multiplied by the bias surface. The result is a surface of relative weights. It tells us which sites are more likely to be sampled than others, and its values are no longer suitability.

Three arguments define the weight:

- `prediction_layer`: the layer of the prediction to use.
- `sampling`: where in the niche the weight is the highest. With `"centroid"` the weight is higher near the centroid, with `"edge"` it is higher near the boundary, and with `"uniform"` it is the same for every cell.
- `method`: the kind of layer used, `"suitability"` or `"mahalanobis"`.

Let's start with the most common case, which is suitability with more weight near the centroid.

```{r apply}
# Applying the bias surface to suitability
biased <- apply_bias(prepared_bias = bias_prep,
                     prediction = pred_rast,
                     prediction_layer = "suitability",
                     sampling = "centroid",
                     method = "suitability",
                     verbose = FALSE)

# Elements in the result
names(biased)

# How the surface was calculated
biased$combination_formula
```

<br>

The result is also a list. The first element is the biased surface, and its name tells us the layer and the sampling that were used. Let's compare the prediction with the biased surface.

```{r apply_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting area parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = 0.7)

# Plots
terra::plot(pred_rast[["suitability"]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Suitability")

terra::plot(biased[[1]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Suitability and Bias")
```

<br>

The suitable area is in the same place, but the weights changed. Sites with suitable conditions and little sampling effort lost most of their weight. The highest values are now in sites that are both suitable and well sampled, and the suitable sites in the north, where fewer species have been recorded, have low values.

A surface obtained this way is included in the package as `applied_bias_rast.tif`. We will draw data points from it in the vignette [4. Generate data](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/generating_data.html).

<br>

### Keeping the weights inside the niche

The layer `suitability` has values far from the niche too. They are tiny, but a data point could still be drawn there. To limit the surface to the niche, we use a truncated layer. `apply_bias()` removes the cells where the prediction is zero, so the cells outside the niche become `NA` and can't be sampled.

```{r apply_trunc}
# Applying the bias surface to truncated suitability
biased_cent <- apply_bias(prepared_bias = bias_prep,
                          prediction = pred_rast,
                          prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc",
                          sampling = "centroid",
                          method = "suitability",
                          verbose = FALSE)

names(biased_cent)
```

<br>

### Effect of the sampling argument

Now let's compare the three options for `sampling`. We will use the truncated layer for all of them. This matters for `"edge"` and `"uniform"`. Without a boundary, the cells far outside the niche would get the highest weight with `"edge"`, and the same weight as any other cell with `"uniform"`.

```{r sampling}
# More weight near the boundary of the niche
biased_edge <- apply_bias(prepared_bias = bias_prep,
                          prediction = pred_rast,
                          prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc",
                          sampling = "edge",
                          method = "suitability",
                          verbose = FALSE)

# The same weight for every cell in the niche
biased_unif <- apply_bias(prepared_bias = bias_prep,
                          prediction = pred_rast,
                          prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc",
                          sampling = "uniform",
                          method = "suitability",
                          verbose = FALSE)

# How each surface was calculated
biased_cent$combination_formula
biased_edge$combination_formula
biased_unif$combination_formula
```

<br>

Let's check how the three surfaces look next to the prediction.

```{r sampling_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting area parameters
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), cex = 0.6)

# Plots
terra::plot(pred_rast[["suitability_trunc"]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Truncated Suitability")

terra::plot(biased_cent[[1]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Bias with Centroid Sampling")

terra::plot(biased_edge[[1]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Bias with Edge Sampling")

terra::plot(biased_unif[[1]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Bias with Uniform Sampling")
```

<br>

As shown in the plots, the three surfaces cover the same area, which is the niche, but the highest weights are in different places. With `"centroid"`, they are in well-sampled sites with conditions close to the centroid. With `"edge"`, they move to well-sampled sites near the boundary of the niche. With `"uniform"`, suitability makes no difference inside the niche, so the surface is the bias itself.

<br>

### Effect of the method argument

A Mahalanobis distance layer can be used in place of suitability. Distance is the lowest at the centroid, so the weight is calculated the other way around: 1 divided by the distance for `"centroid"`, and the distance itself for `"edge"`. The argument `method` tells the function which kind of layer it is receiving.

```{r method}
# Applying the bias surface to truncated Mahalanobis distance
biased_maha <- apply_bias(prepared_bias = bias_prep,
                          prediction = pred_rast,
                          prediction_layer = "Mahalanobis_trunc",
                          sampling = "centroid",
                          method = "mahalanobis",
                          verbose = FALSE)

# How the surface was calculated
biased_maha$combination_formula
```

<br>

The method has to agree with the layer. The function checks the name of the layer, and it stops if the name says one kind of layer and `method` says the other, because the weight would end up in the wrong part of the niche.

```{r method_fail, error = TRUE}
# A suitability layer with the method for Mahalanobis distance
biased_wrong <- apply_bias(prepared_bias = bias_prep,
                           prediction = pred_rast,
                           prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc",
                           sampling = "centroid",
                           method = "mahalanobis",
                           verbose = FALSE)
```

<br>

Let's plot the surfaces obtained with the two methods, both with `"centroid"`.

```{r method_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting area parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = 0.7)

# Plots
terra::plot(biased_cent[[1]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Method: Suitability")

terra::plot(biased_maha[[1]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Method: Mahalanobis")
```

<br>

Both surfaces give more weight to sites near the centroid, but the patterns are different. With Mahalanobis distance, the few cells that are almost at the centroid get weights much higher than all the others, so most of the map looks dark. To learn what this means for the data points, see [The two methods give different patterns](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/concepts.html#the-two-methods-give-different-patterns) in the Concepts vignette.

<br>

```{r par_reset}
# Reset plotting parameters
par(original_par)
```

<br>

## Save and import

The biased surfaces are `SpatRaster` objects. They can be saved with `terra::writeRaster()` and imported with `terra::rast()`.

```{r save_import, eval=FALSE}
# file name (in a temporary directory for demonstration purposes)
temp_raster <- file.path(tempdir(), "applied_bias_rast.tif")

# Save the biased surface to a local directory
terra::writeRaster(biased[[1]], filename = temp_raster, overwrite = TRUE)

# Import the biased surface from a local directory
biased_imported <- terra::rast(temp_raster)
```

<br>

The next step is to draw data points from these surfaces. See the vignette [4. Generate data](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/generating_data.html).
